title: Why version control exists
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what a commit is, why every professional team keeps its work in Git, and what problem it solves that copying folders never did.

blocks.text: Before version control, keeping history meant copying the folder: report-v2, report-v2-final, report-v2-final-ACTUAL. Everyone recognises it because everyone has done it. It fails at exactly the moment it matters — when two people edit at once, when you need what the file looked like on Tuesday, or when something broke and nobody can say which change did it.
Git replaces all of that with one idea: a project keeps its own history, and every meaningful state of that project gets recorded deliberately.
A commit is a labelled snapshot

A commit records what every tracked file looked like at one moment, who recorded it, when, and a message saying why. That last part is what turns a backup into a history: the file tells you what changed, the message tells you what it was for.

blocks.caption: What a history actually looks like
lines: 8b02e5d  2026-08-13  Malee    Add rate limit to the login route
1d77af0  2026-08-13  Songpon  Fix timezone on the report export

items: Each line is one deliberate save point, not an automatic backup
The short code at the front is that commit's permanent identity
Any commit can be looked at, compared, or returned to, at any time

blocks.text: Distributed: everyone has the whole history

When you copy a Git project, you get every commit ever made, not just the current files. That is why you can read history, compare versions, and commit while offline on a plane. The shared server is a meeting point, not the only copy — and it means the loss of that server is an inconvenience rather than a catastrophe.

blocks.title: What this buys you day to day
blocks.text: Three questions become answerable in seconds: what changed, when did it change, and who changed it. Without a history, all three are guesswork — and the third one turns into blame instead of investigation.

A repository is an audit trail of every change to a system's source. When something malicious appears in a codebase, the history is what lets you say when it entered and through which change. Teams that do not keep one are left comparing files against memory.

blocks.title: History cuts both ways
blocks.text: Anything committed is preserved. Delete a password in the next commit and the original is still there in the earlier one, permanently, for anyone who can read the repository. That is why a later lesson is entirely about what must never be committed in the first place.

blocks.title: Check what you have
steps: Run: git --version          (install it if this fails)
blocks.expected: A version number, then your identity recorded in Git's global configuration. Every commit you make from now on carries that name and email — which is why setting it correctly matters before your first commit rather than after.

cheatsheet: A commit = a snapshot of tracked files + author + time + a message saying why
The message is what turns a backup into a usable history
Git is distributed: a copy contains the entire history, not just current files
You can commit and read history with no network at all
History answers what changed, when, and by whom — in seconds
Anything committed is preserved, including a secret you delete later
git config --global user.name and user.email identify your commits

checkpoint.prompt: What does a single commit record?

choices.A: A snapshot of the tracked files at that moment, plus who made it, when, and a message saying why
choices.B: Only the lines that changed in one file
choices.C: A reminder to save your work later
choices.D: A copy of the whole project folder including ignored files

checkpoint.explanation: The snapshot plus the metadata is the unit. The message is the part that makes the history readable months later.

checkpoint.prompt: What does it mean that Git is distributed?

choices.A: Every copy of the project contains the full history
choices.B: Each person gets a different part of the code
choices.C: The files are split across several servers

checkpoint.explanation: You can read it and commit offline A clone is a complete copy of the history. The shared server is a coordination point, not the sole holder of the project.

checkpoint.prompt: You commit a file containing a password, notice, and delete it in the very next commit. What is the situation?

choices.A: Only the server copy still has it
choices.B: The password is gone, because the current files no longer contain it
choices.C: The password remains in the earlier commit and is readable by anyone with the repository

checkpoint.explanation: History preserves what was committed. Removing it going forward does not remove it from the past — the credential must be treated as exposed and rotated.
